viblio-introducing-credibility-signals-a.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: How do viewers assess YouTube credibility, and how can citations support that assessment?

methods.text: Twelve contextual-inquiry interviews informed a citation prototype, followed by a reflective evaluation with twelve participants.

findings.text: Participants combined channel information, production quality, and prior knowledge, but encountered weaknesses in existing signals.
Evaluation participants found the prototype useful and intuitive for assessing credibility.

contributions.text: A viewer-facing prototype links supporting, refuting, and contextual sources to specific moments in videos.

limitations.text: Large-scale adoption and defenses against malicious or low-quality citations remain untested directions for future work.

echo-chambers-information-brokers-truth-.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: How does the structure of Truth Social interactions shift around major political events?

methods.text: Re-truth network analysis examines centrality and community structure around the Roe v. Wade decision and the Mar-a-Lago search.

findings.text: A small set of highly central accounts shapes attention, while bridging accounts connect otherwise separated regions.
Both events coincide with temporary consolidation followed by fragmentation; their trajectories differ.

contributions.text: A cyclical account connects event-driven consolidation, influencer prominence, and recurring fragmentation.

limitations.text: The sample favors active accounts; incomplete follower access limits reconstruction. Reposts do not establish user intent, and the study does not test the ranking algorithm.

ephemeral-feeds-and-enduring-rituals.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: Who participates in RushTok, how do they relate to its community, and what stakes accompany visibility?

methods.text: A mixed-methods survey of 71 respondents is combined with a reflexive account of unsuccessful creator recruitment.

findings.text: Many respondents recognized a community (51/71), but only 11/71 identified as members.
Creator-centered attention and entertainment support participation without necessarily producing membership.

contributions.text: RushTok illustrates a community assembled around an offline ritual and sustained through recommendation.

limitations.text: Convenience recruitment, self-report, a predominantly female audience sample, and no completed creator interviews limit generalization and triangulation.

echoes-in-the-algorithm.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: How accurately do people infer relative TikTok reach without metrics, and how do those judgments align with preference?

methods.text: TokOrNot elicited 3,513 paired-video judgments from 363 U.S. adults, benchmarked against verified public view counts.

findings.text: Higher-reach identification was 56.75% (95% CI 56.01-58.55); preference and prediction matched in 83.48% of trials (95% CI 83.12-85.95).

contributions.text: An empirical benchmark examines judgments of observable reach under hidden metrics rather than the recommender itself.

limitations.text: Fixed preference-first question order may anchor reach judgments. View counts are a bounded reach proxy; the task and older adult sample do not represent everyday TikTok use in full.

misinformation-or-activism-mapping-netwo.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: Who posts under #SaveTheChildren, what tactics do they use, and which motivations and actions do they advocate?

methods.text: Five researchers iteratively coded 1,400 Instagram posts collected across four hashtags during 2020.

findings.text: Accounts used differing visual and rhetorical strategies to circulate conspiracy narratives under a child-protection frame.

contributions.text: The case connects identity, moral authority, and misinformation within networked moral panic.

examining-mainstream-news-media-narrativ.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: What youth online-safety narratives appear in mainstream news, and how do they compare with academic research?

methods.text: A PRISMA-guided review screened 306 articles to 157 textual articles from selected U.S. mainstream outlets (2020-2024); researchers used deductive thematic analysis and consensus coding.

findings.text: The corpus emphasizes negative risk experiences and mental-health concerns rather than positive online experiences.
Parental control and legislative restrictions dominate suggested interventions, with minimal youth participation.
Adult stakeholders dominate quoted perspectives; direct youth input is rare.

contributions.text: Comparison with academic research motivates youth participation, digital literacy, and developmentally appropriate parental mediation as recommendations, not experimentally tested interventions.

examining-mainstream-news-media-narrativ.coverageNote: Verified against the full paper supplied by the author. No separate limitations section is present; the scope note describes the reported study design rather than an author-stated limitations list.

limitations.text: Scope of evidence: the selected textual news corpus is not a direct study of youth experiences or a causal test of media effects.

introducing-credibility-signals-and-cita.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: How should credibility information be presented on YouTube search and playback pages?

methods.text: Initial interviews inform designs for credibility signals and time-linked citations, with further studies proposed.

findings.text: Initial interviews indicate that video intent and context shape how people would use credibility signals.

contributions.text: Early interface proposals explore third-party information and citations within YouTube.

limitations.text: The survey and extension deployment are planned work in this paper, not completed evaluations.

rushtok-an-evaluation-of-event-based-com.summaryType: Editorial paraphrases with source locators; not quotations.

questions.text: How do event-based TikTok communities form, and how do creators and viewers understand participation?

methods.text: The statement describes ongoing qualitative content coding and proposes creator interviews and a viewer survey.

contributions.text: An early research agenda uses RushTok to study algorithmically assembled, event-based communities.

limitations.text: This statement proposes future studies and does not report the completed 2026 survey findings.
